solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Game board flipped with a note of disapproval

indicators.note: flipped means the word for board is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: board, as in 'bed and board', is one's keep
a boo is a jeer of disapproval

explanation.surface: A board game whose board was overturned, greeted with a jeer from a player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'board' here is food and lodging, as in 'room and board', not a games board; 'flipped' reads it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Peekaboo is a game played with babies, hiding and revealing one's face.

clue.text: Acquire funds when full of drink

indicators.note: full of means holding inside, so the drink goes into the funds word

parts.note: a purse is a sum of money, as in a prize purse
cha is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: Buying things with money while drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA is British slang for tea; 'full of' puts it into PURSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To purchase is to buy, that is to get something by paying.

clue.text: One who is damn enthusiastic, so to speak

definitions.text: One who is damn enthusiastic, so to speak

parts.words: One who is damn enthusiastic, so to speak
parts.note: damn, said aloud, is dam: an animal keen on building dams, and a very keen person

explanation.surface: A description of someone extremely keen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damn' sounds like dam: beavers build dams, and the phrase means a very zealous worker.
explanation.definitionFit: An eager beaver is an idiom for an over-keen, hard-working person.

clue.text: Busy man hosts contest working for king

indicators.note: hosts means holds inside, so the contest goes into the mixed-up letters
busy suggests bustling activity, so the letters of man are stirred about

parts.note: a game is a contest
on means working or functioning

explanation.surface: A busy man stages a contest while serving a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busy' scrambles the man letters to AMN, and 'hosts' opens that up after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Agamemnon was the legendary Greek king who led the army at Troy.

clue.text: Huge round insects having turned tail

parts.note: O is round in shape

indicators.note: having turned tail means the end of the insect word is turned about, a letter shifting at the tail

parts.note: bees are insects

explanation.surface: A swarm of round insects flees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having turned tail' swaps the last two letters of BEES, moving an E to the end to give BESE.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means very overweight, so enormous in size.

clue.text: Drive three-quarters inebriated

indicators.note: three-quarters means only six of the eight letters of the drunk word are kept, the last two dropped

parts.note: hammered is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A warning about driving after drinking most of the way to drunkenness.
explanation.walkthrough: HAMMERED (slang for drunk) loses its last quarter, ED, by 'three-quarters'.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive a nail is to hammer it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Version of 7 journalist is packing

indicators.note: a version of something is a reworking, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: 7 is the answer to 7 down, MAR
ED, short for editor, is the crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A journalist carries a version of another clue's answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Version of' rearranges MAR to ARM.
explanation.definitionFit: Packing is slang for carrying a gun, so it means armed.

clue.text: Boozer ultimately overcome by mother's ruin

indicators.note: overcome by puts the boozer's letter beneath the mother word in the down entry

parts.note: ma is mother

indicators.note: ultimately takes the final letter of the drinker

explanation.surface: A drinker succumbs to mother's ruin, slang for gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mother's ruin' is British slang for gin, which suits 'Boozer'; split, 'mother' gives MA and 'ruin' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar is to spoil or damage, so to ruin.

clue.text: Verses maybe in Frost broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means sent out over the air, so the frost word is spoken

parts.note: rime is hoar frost

explanation.surface: Poems, perhaps by Robert Frost, read on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frost' tempts as the poet but is RIME, hoar frost; 'broadcast' gives its sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhyme is a short poem, so verses are an example of it.

clue.text: Cohabitee left feeding Big Mama briefly

indicators.note: feeding means going into, so the left letter goes inside

parts.note: big means fat

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the mother word loses its last letter

parts.note: mater is an old-fashioned British word for mother

explanation.surface: A housemate's left in charge of feeding a large mother.
explanation.walkthrough: Mater is old British public-school slang for mother; 'briefly' drops its last letter, and 'feeding' puts the left letter into the big word.
explanation.definitionFit: A flatmate shares an apartment with you, so is someone you live with.

clue.text: Remark about Edgar being dishevelled

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: dishevelled means messed up, so the letters of the name are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone comments on Edgar's untidy appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being dishevelled' rearranges EDGAR into GRADE. 'Remark' is read as re-mark, to mark again.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-mark an exam paper is to regrade it, assessing it a second time.

clue.text: Bivalves discovered near quarry? It's a bit fishy

indicators.note: discovered is read as dis-covered, the outer letters of the shellfish word stripped off

parts.note: clams are bivalve molluscs
quarry, a hunted animal, is prey

explanation.surface: Shellfish found close to a stone quarry seem suspicious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovered' strips C and S from CLAMS, leaving LAM, beside PREY. The lamprey is a jawless, eel-like creature, only partly a true fish, hence 'a bit fishy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamprey is an eel-like jawless vertebrate, fish-like enough to be called somewhat fishy.

clue.text: Stable source of protein

parts.note: a dependable food staple, but read as meat from an animal kept in a stable

explanation.surface: A reliable item in a healthy diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' seems to mean reliable, but it is the building where horses live.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat from horses, which are housed in stables, is a protein food in some countries.

clue.text: Agent retired finally to become writer

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn, so the word for agent goes backwards

parts.note: a fed is an American federal agent

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of each of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A spy hangs up the trench coat and takes up the pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns FED back to DEF; 'finally' takes O and E from 'to' and 'become'.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Defoe was the English novelist who wrote Robinson Crusoe.

clue.text: New roofer's lad around noon fetching a 22 5?

indicators.note: around means the jumbled letters go round the noon letter
new means made afresh, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A roofer's apprentice is sent for a glass hammer around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' makes FOOLSERRAD from ROOFER'S LAD, and 'around' puts it round N. 22 and 5 are GLASS and HAMMER: an apprentice sent for a glass hammer is on a hoax.
explanation.definitionFit: A fool's errand is a pointless task, like a prank on a new worker sent for a nonexistent tool.

clue.text: Part of Ship Street regularly out of herring

indicators.note: regularly out of picks every second letter from the fish word

explanation.surface: A street in a fishing port where the herring catch has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly out of' takes the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of hErRiNg: ERN.
explanation.definitionFit: The stern is the rear section of a vessel.

clue.text: Defender starts to intimidate opposite number after bite

indicators.note: after places the initials behind the word for bite

parts.note: to champ is to bite or chew noisily

indicators.note: starts to takes the opening letter of each of the next three words

explanation.surface: A footballer bites an opponent to scare him.
explanation.walkthrough: CHAMP (bite) comes first, then 'starts to' gives I, O, N from 'intimidate opposite number'.
explanation.definitionFit: A champion is one who fights for or defends a cause, or a title holder defending it.

clue.text: Fabric caught on tree at top of lake

indicators.note: at top of puts the tree above the lake in the down entry

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
an ash is a tree
a mere is a lake

explanation.surface: Cloth snagged on a tree at the head of a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is a fine wool cloth made from goat hair.

clue.text: Suckers in jumpers put on the wrong way?

indicators.note: the wrong way means using the opposite action, so pull becomes push in the sweater word

parts.note: jumpers are sweaters, or pullovers

explanation.surface: Fools who put their sweaters on back to front.
explanation.walkthrough: PULLOVERS, with PULL swapped for its opposite PUSH, gives the answer; 'jumpers' is British for sweaters.
explanation.definitionFit: Pushovers are people easily fooled or beaten, and suckers are gullible people.

clue.text: Carriages should primarily shelter reps in transit

indicators.note: primarily takes the first letter of the word after it

parts.note: lee is shelter from the wind

indicators.note: in transit means on the move, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Train cars ought first to give sales reps somewhere to sit when travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in transit' rearranges REPS to PERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleepers are railway carriages with berths for overnight travel.

clue.text: Wind instruments collected by eastern church vanish

indicators.note: collected by means held inside, so the vanes sit within the eastern church letters

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
weather vanes are instruments showing the wind's direction

explanation.surface: Flutes and oboes gathered by an Orthodox church disappear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind instruments' suggests flutes but means weather vanes; 'collected by' puts them inside the eastern and Church of England letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To evanesce is to fade away to nothing, a literary word for disappearing.

clue.text: Plant species is alien to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A botanist notes that a certain species is not native here.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is an agave grown for its tough fibre, used in rope.

clue.text: Child skinning both snakes and amphibians

indicators.note: skinning both means each of the two animal words loses its outer letters

parts.note: asps are venomous snakes
frogs are amphibians

explanation.surface: A grisly picture of a child flaying snakes and frogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skinning both' strips ASPS to SP and FROGS to ROG.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprog is British slang for a child or baby.

clue.text: Diviner welcomes daughter's ceremonial meal

indicators.note: welcomes means takes in, so the daughter letter goes inside

parts.note: a seer is a diviner who foresees the future

explanation.surface: A fortune teller welcomes her daughter to a ritual dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Seder is the Jewish ritual feast held at the start of Passover.

clue.text: Witness algae engulfing upturned vessel

indicators.note: upturned in a down clue means the hidden letters read from bottom to top
engulfing says the two words hold the answer's letters inside them

explanation.surface: A witness sees algae swamping a capsized boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engulfing' hides SSALG across 'Witness algae', and 'upturned' reads it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass is a drinking vessel, a container for liquid.

clue.text: Scary girl mistaking Rouen for another city

parts.note: Scary Spice of the Spice Girls is Mel B, Melanie Brown

indicators.note: mistaking means getting it wrong, so the letters of the French city are jumbled

explanation.surface: A frightening girl confuses Rouen with somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: MEL B is Scary Spice of the Spice Girls pop group; 'mistaking' rearranges ROUEN to OURNE. The definition contrasts the answer with Rouen.
explanation.definitionFit: Melbourne is a city in Australia, a different one from the French Rouen.

clue.text: Respite from the French 7 in Revolution

parts.note: le is French for the
7 is MAR, which reversed by in Revolution becomes ram, and a tup is a ram

explanation.surface: A pause from France's ruin during the Revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: MAR (7) turned round by 'in Revolution' is RAM, which is a TUP, a British word for a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-up is a pause or easing off, a break from effort.

clue.text: Misery of O'Connor and Lynam collaboration?

parts.note: Des O'Connor and Des Lynam were both British TV presenters named Des
two people working together make a pair

explanation.surface: Two TV hosts team up, to unhappy results.
explanation.walkthrough: Des O'Connor was a British singer and chat-show host; Des Lynam a British sports presenter. Together they make a Des pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Despair is utter hopelessness, a deep misery.

clue.text: Queen leaving banger for relative

indicators.note: leaving means going away, so the queen letters drop out of the firework

parts.note: a squib is a small firework, and banger is British for a firecracker

explanation.surface: The Queen walks out on a sausage for a family member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banger' suggests the British sausage but is a firework, SQUIB.
explanation.definitionFit: Sib is short for sibling, a brother or sister.

clue.text: Juvenile eaten up and giraffe eviscerated

indicators.note: up here means stirred up, so the letters of the eating word are rearranged
eviscerated means gutted, so only the outer letters of the animal remain

explanation.surface: A young animal is devoured and a giraffe is disembowelled on safari.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' rearranges EATEN into TEENA; 'eviscerated' leaves G and E of giraffe.
explanation.definitionFit: A teenage person is adolescent, still young.

clue.text: Sturdy vehicle obscured by rhubarb

indicators.note: obscured by means hidden inside, so the vehicle sits within the nonsense word

parts.note: rhubarb is British slang for nonsense, as is rot
a bus is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A tough vehicle disappears behind a rhubarb patch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rhubarb' looks like the plant but is British slang for nonsense; 'obscured by' hides the vehicle inside that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Robust means strong and hardy, the same as sturdy.

clue.text: Poetry on record is in instalments

indicators.note: on places the poems after the record letters in the across entry

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
odes are poems

explanation.surface: A spoken-word record of poems released in parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Episodes are separate parts of a serial, each one delivered in turn.
